questions.stemText:
In the Rutherford $\alpha$-particle scattering experiment, $\alpha$-particles are directed at a thin gold foil.

Which is a direct deduction from the results of the experiment?

A The $\alpha$-particles are negatively charged.
B The $\alpha$-particles are positively charged.
C The atom consists of a large amount of empty space.
D The proton number of the gold nucleus is 79.

questions.difficultyReason: It asks for the standard inference from most alpha particles passing through the foil.
questions.misconception: Confusing known projectile properties with experimental deductions

explanation.body: Most alpha particles passed through the thin foil with little or no deflection. The rare large deflections show that the region producing strong scattering occupies very little of each atom, so most of the atom is empty space.

perOption.A: Alpha particles are positively charged.
perOption.B: The positive charge of the incident alpha particles was already known.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The observation that most particles pass through does not determine gold’s exact proton number.

The experiment is repeated with a foil made from a heavier isotope of gold. How would the results be different? A There would be no significant change. B A much greater proportion of the alpha-particles would be back-scattered. C A much greater proportion of the alpha-particles would be deflected through a large angle. D A greater proportion of the alpha-particles would pass through with no significant deviation.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: A much greater proportion of the alpha-particles would be deflected through a large angle.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student applies the unchanged nuclear charge of an isotope to Rutherford scattering.
questions.misconception: Assuming extra neutrons increase nuclear charge

explanation.body: Most alpha particles still pass through with negligible deviation because atoms are mainly empty space. The heavier isotope has the same nuclear charge, and the chance of a nearly head-on encounter is approximately unchanged. The scattering pattern therefore shows no significant change.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Extra neutrons leave the nuclear charge and the chance of near-head-on scattering essentially unchanged.
perOption.C: The higher nuclear mass does not substantially strengthen the Coulomb repulsion responsible for large deflections.
perOption.D: Changing the isotope does not appreciably change the chance of an encounter that deflects an alpha particle.

Which observation shows that a radioactive source emits only $\alpha$-radiation?

A. The count rate reduces significantly 1 cm away from the source in air.
B. The count rate reduces significantly when the source is surrounded by a lead block.
C. The radiation beam is deflected by an electric field perpendicular to it.
D. The radiation beam remains undeflected by a magnetic field parallel to it.

stemImage.alt: Question 30: Which observation shows that a radioactive source emits only α-radiation?

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The intended answer relies on recognising the short range of alpha radiation in air.
questions.misconception: Treating electric deflection as unique to alpha particles

explanation.body: The key selects the large drop in count rate over $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ of air because alpha radiation has a short range in air. Beta and gamma radiation are more penetrating, so the key uses the short-distance drop as the distinguishing observation.

perOption.A: Correct. Alpha radiation has a short range in air.
perOption.B: A lead block can shield alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
perOption.C: Both alpha and beta particles are charged and deflect in a perpendicular electric field.

What is the activity of the sample after another 3 years?
questions.stemText: The activity of a radioactive sample decreases to one third of its original activity Ao in a period of 3 years. What is the activity of the sample after another 3 years? A 0.11 $A_{o}$ B 0.17 $A_{o}$ C 0.33 $A_{o}$ D 0.67 $A_{o}$

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recognise that equal time intervals multiply activity by the same factor.
questions.misconception: Treating exponential decay as linear

explanation.body: For radioactive decay, $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$. At three years, $A_0/3=A_0e^{-3\lambda}$, so $\lambda=\ln(1/3)/(-3)=0.36620\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. At six years, $A=A_0e^{-0.36620(6)}\approx0.11A_0$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the second three-year interval as one half-life.
perOption.C: Gives the activity after only three years.
perOption.D: Gives the fraction lost in the first three years.

questions.misconception: Overestimating the frequency of backscattering

explanation.body: Most alpha particles pass through the foil undeflected, so $n$ peaks sharply at $0^\circ$. Very few particles are deflected through large angles, so the count rate stays low at large positive and negative angles.

perOption.A: This puts the highest rates near backscattering angles and misses the strong undeviated beam.
perOption.B: This gives backscattering peaks comparable to the forward peak even though backscattering is rare.
perOption.C: Correct. A narrow forward peak dominates the low counts at large angles.

Today, the activity of a sample of caesium−137 is 4.0 x $10^{5}$ Bq. The half-life of caesium−137 is 33 years.

What is the best estimate of the number of caesium−137 nuclei that will decay in the next two days?
questions.stemText: Today, the activity of a sample of caesium−137 is 4.0 x 105 Bq. The half-life of caesium−137 is 33 years. What is the best estimate of the number of caesium−137 nuclei that will decay in the next two days? A 5.0 x $10^{8}$ B 1.2 x $10^{9}$ C 6.9 x $10^{10}$ D 9.5 x $10^{12}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper
grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must justify constant activity over two days and convert the duration to seconds.
questions.misconception: Using becquerels with a duration in days

explanation.body: Two days is very short compared with the 33-year half-life, so the activity is effectively constant. Activity is the number of decays per unit time, giving $N_{\mathrm{decay}}\approx At=(4.0\times10^5)(2\times24\times3600)=6.912\times10^{10}$ decays.

perOption.A: This undercounts the decays by using an effective duration far shorter than two days.
perOption.B: This is close to what results from using the number of minutes in two days as the number of seconds.
perOption.C: Correct. The activity times the elapsed seconds gives about 69 billion decays.
perOption.D: This would require a much larger activity or a much longer time than given.

A Releasing a photon of energy $2\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
B Releasing a photon of energy $3\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
C Capturing a photon of energy $2\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
D Capturing a photon of energy $3\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

grail:19921 SAJC Prelim H2 P1 2025_Qn and Ans

questions.difficultyReason: The student must compare rest masses and convert the mass difference to an energy threshold.
questions.misconception: Confusing binding energy with energy released during breakup

explanation.body: The combined rest mass of the proton and neutron exceeds that of the deuteron, so the reaction needs an energy input. The mass difference is $(1.0086+1.0097-2.0150)\ \mathrm{u}=0.0033\ \mathrm{u}$. Using $E=\Delta mc^2$ gives about $3.07\ \mathrm{MeV}$, rounded to $3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ in the key.

perOption.B: Even a 3 MeV emitted photon would carry energy away from the breakup.
perOption.C: A 2 MeV photon supplies less than the binding energy.

questions.stem: Which combination of successive emissions produces a final nucleus with the same proton number as the starting nucleus?
questions.stemText: Which combination of successive emissions produces a final nucleus with the same proton number as the starting nucleus? A α α β B α β β C α β γ D β γ β

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must add the proton-number changes associated with successive emissions.
questions.misconception: Reversing the proton-number change in beta-minus decay

explanation.body: Alpha decay decreases the proton number by 2, beta-minus decay increases it by 1, and gamma emission leaves it unchanged. One alpha emission followed by two beta-minus emissions gives a net change of $-2+1+1=0$.

perOption.A: Two alpha emissions and one beta-minus emission give a net change of −3.
perOption.B: Correct. The changes cancel.
perOption.C: One alpha and one beta-minus emission give a net change of −1, and gamma emission leaves it unchanged.
perOption.D: Two beta-minus emissions raise the proton number by 2, and gamma emission leaves it unchanged.

questions.stem:
A nucleus X decays into a nucleus Y by emitting an alpha particle followed by two beta particles.

Which statement about this nuclear decay is correct?
questions.stemText: A nucleus X decays into a nucleus Y by emitting an alpha particle followed by two beta particles. Which statement about this nuclear decay is correct? A Beta particle decay occurs when an orbital electron is emitted. B Nucleus Y has the same nucleon number as nucleus X. C Nucleus Y is an isotope of nucleus X. D The total mass of the products is equal to the mass of the initial nucleus X.

options.label: A
options.text: Beta particle decay occurs when an orbital electron is emitted.

options.label: B
options.text: Nucleus Y has the same nucleon number as nucleus X.

options.label: C
options.text: Nucleus Y is an isotope of nucleus X.

options.label: D
options.text: The total mass of the products is equal to the mass of the initial nucleus X.

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: Tracks proton and nucleon numbers through three emissions.
questions.misconception: Confusing proton number with nucleon number

explanation.body: The key tracks the charged products using $\vphantom{X}{}^{a}_{b}\mathrm{X}\to{}^{a-4}_{b}\mathrm{Y}+{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}+2\,{}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$. X and Y have the same proton number and different neutron numbers, so Y is an isotope of X.

perOption.A: A beta-minus electron is produced when a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton.
perOption.B: Alpha emission lowers the daughter nucleus's nucleon number by four.
perOption.C: Correct. Y has the same proton number and four fewer neutrons.
perOption.D: The products carry kinetic energy, so their total rest mass is smaller.

questions.stemText: Nucleus P decays in two stages to produce nucleus Q. Which decay sequence will result in the highest number of neutrons in nucleus Q? A a $\beta$-particle followed by a $\gamma$-ray B an $\alpha$-particle followed by a $\gamma$-ray C an $\alpha$-particle followed by a $\beta$-particle D a $\beta$-particle followed by another $\beta$-particle

stemImage.alt: Question 29: Nucleus P decays in two stages to produce nucleus Q. Which decay sequence will result in the highest number of neutrons in nucleus Q?

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Tracking the neutron number change for each decay type.
questions.misconception: Thinking β-decay leaves the neutron number unchanged or that γ emission changes the nucleus composition

explanation.body: Let R be the intermediate nucleus. Beta decay gives $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{P}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}+{}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$, followed by gamma decay $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{Q}+\gamma$. The neutron number in Q is $A-(Z+1)=A-Z-1$.

perOption.A: Correct. The neutron count drops by just one.
perOption.B: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and gamma emission leaves the neutron count unchanged.
perOption.C: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and beta-minus decay converts one more into a proton.
perOption.D: Each beta-minus decay converts a neutron to a proton, so the count drops by two.

questions.stem:
A radioactive source is placed near a detector and the reading is 324 counts per minute. After two half-lives, the reading drops to 108 counts per minute.

What is the background radiation in counts per minute?
questions.stemText: A radioactive source is placed near a detector and the reading is 324 counts per minute. After two half-lives, the reading drops to 108 counts per minute. What is the background radiation in counts per minute? A 27 B 36 C 54 D 72

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires separating the constant background from the decaying source count over two half-lives.
questions.misconception: Halving the total count rate, including background, each half-life

explanation.body: Let $C$ be the initial count rate due to the source alone. After two half-lives it has fallen by $3C/4$, so $3C/4=324-108$ and $C=288\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$. The background count rate is $324-288=36\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Quarters the later reading even though it includes a constant background contribution.
perOption.B: Correct. The background contributes 36 counts per minute.
perOption.C: Halves the later reading even though the half-life applies only to the source contribution.
perOption.D: Gives the remaining source count rate after two half-lives.

explanation.body: Use the given nuclear mass to find the mass defect: $\Delta m=[82(1.00863)+57(1.00728)-138.955]\ \mathrm{u}=1.16762\ \mathrm{u}$. What fraction of a sample would remain after 16 hours?
questions.stemText: The half-life of a certain radioactive isotope is 32 hours. What fraction of a sample would remain after 16 hours? A 0.25 B 0.29 C 0.5 D 0.71

appearances.originalFile: grail:10439 CJC.H2.PRELIM.2023.P1.QP

questions.difficultyReason: The student must apply the decay factor for half of a half-life.
questions.misconception: Confusing fraction decayed with fraction remaining

explanation.body: Use $x=x_0(\tfrac12)^n$, where $n$ is the number of elapsed half-lives. In $16$ hours, $n=16/32=0.5$, so $x=x_0(\tfrac12)^{0.5}=0.7071x_0\approx0.71x_0$.

perOption.A: Treats 16 hours as two half-lives by reversing the time ratio.
perOption.B: Gives the fraction that decayed.
perOption.C: Gives the fraction remaining after a full half-life.
perOption.D: Correct.

A radioactive sample consists of two nuclides.

One has a half-life of $48\ \mathrm{h}$ and decays by emitting alpha particles, while the other has a half-life of $36\ \mathrm{h}$ and emits beta particles.

The initial count rate is $352\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. When a sheet of paper is placed between the source and the detector, the count rate becomes $256\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. The background count rate is $16\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

What will the count rate be after 6 days, without the paper present?

A. $27\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
B. $36\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
C. $43\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
D. $52\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 29: A radioactive sample consists of two nuclides. One has a half-life of 48 h and decays by emitting alpha particles, while the other has a half-life of 36 h and e

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires isolating two source rates, decaying them separately and restoring the background.
questions.misconception: Applying radioactive decay to background counts

explanation.body:
Paper stops alpha particles, so the initial alpha count rate is $352-256=96\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and the initial beta count rate is $256-16=240\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Six days is $144\ \mathrm{h}$, or three alpha half-lives and four beta half-lives.

perOption.A: Leaves out the background count at the detector.
perOption.B: Undercounts the source contribution, for example by applying too many half-lives.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overcounts the source contribution by allowing too little decay.

The count rate drops sharply when paper is inserted, so the radiation is stopped by paper: it must be $\alpha$ radiation, which has low penetrating power.

The remaining $24\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ is the background count rate, so the initial count rate due to the source is $532 - 24 = 508\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

After two half-lives the source count rate is $\tfrac{1}{4}(508) = 127\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$, so the reading is $127 + 24 = 151\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct radiation, but forgets to add the background count back to the reading.
perOption.B: $\beta$ radiation would not be stopped by paper, and the background is not added back.
perOption.C: Correct. $\alpha$; $\tfrac{1}{4}(532-24) + 24 = 151\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: $\beta$ radiation would pass through paper.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
It is observed that α-particles incident on a thin gold foil are mostly undeflected, while a small proportion of them are deflected at very large angles.

Which statement provides the explanation for these observations?

A The α-particles are scattered by electrons.
B The α-particles are diffracted by the crystal lattice.
C The α-particles collide with small but massive nuclei.
D The α-particles undergo nuclear fission.

stemImage.alt: Question 29: It is observed that -particles incident on a thin gold foil are mostly undeflected, while a small proportion of them are deflected at very large angles. Which

appearances.originalFile: grail:19911 TMJC_2025_H2 Physics_P1_QP

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the conclusion of Rutherford's scattering experiment.

explanation.body:
Most α-particles pass through undeflected or with only small deflections, so the chance of an α-particle getting close to the positive charge is small: the atom is mostly empty space.

A small fraction (<1%) are deflected through large angles, and a few bounce back close to 180°. Such large deflections need a large force, so all the positive charge must be concentrated in a nucleus that is tiny compared with the atom.

Hence the nucleus is small and very massive.

perOption.A: Electrons are far too light to deflect a massive α-particle through large angles.
perOption.B: Diffraction by the lattice would give a regular pattern, not rare large-angle scattering; the effect is due to Coulomb repulsion by nuclei.
perOption.C: Correct. A small, massive, positive nucleus explains both observations.
perOption.D: Fission is not involved; the α-particles are simply scattered.

questions.stem:
A radioactive sample is placed in a vacuum together with a Geiger Muller (GM) tube. The GM tube is placed 10 cm from the sample and the initial count rate is 1000 $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Several materials are then placed between the sample and GM tube, and the results are shown below.

What radiation is being emitted by the sample?
questions.stemText: A radioactive sample is placed in a vacuum together with a Geiger Muller (GM) tube. The GM tube is placed 10 cm from the sample and the initial count rate is 1000 s–1. Several materials are then placed between the sample and GM tube, and the results are shown below. count rate / s–1 material 0.1 mm aluminium sheet 500 7 mm aluminium sheet 500 10 cm of lead near zero What radiation is being emitted by the sample? A alpha radiation only B beta radiation only C beta and gamma radiation D alpha and gamma radiation

appearances.originalFile: grail:19911 TMJC_2025_H2 Physics_P1_QP

questions.difficultyReason: Requires interpreting count-rate data against known penetrating powers, a standard exercise.
questions.misconception: Thinking a few mm of aluminium does not stop β

explanation.body:
Typical stopping materials: α is stopped by about $10^{-2}$ mm of aluminium or a few cm of air; β by about 5 mm of aluminium; γ by about 100 mm of lead.

The 0.1 mm aluminium sheet halves the count rate, so α radiation must be present and is blocked by the sheet.

The 7 mm aluminium sheet has no further effect, so β radiation is absent.

The 10 cm of lead reduces the count rate to nearly zero, so γ radiation must be present.

perOption.A: With α only, the 0.1 mm aluminium would stop everything; 500 counts per second still get through until the lead.
perOption.B: β would be stopped by 7 mm of aluminium, but the count rate is unchanged from 0.1 mm to 7 mm.
perOption.C: β would be stopped by the 7 mm sheet, and something must be stopped by 0.1 mm of aluminium (only α is).
perOption.D: Correct. α is stopped by thin aluminium; γ passes through aluminium and is stopped by thick lead.

Which of the nuclides P, Q, R and S is the initial nuclide that, after two successive decays, becomes Y?

Four other nuclides, P, Q, R and S are shown on the diagram. S R Which of the nuclides P, Q, R and S is the initial nuclide that, after two successive decays, becomes Y? A P B Q C R D S

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Translate the two decay types into grid displacements and identify the parent two steps from Y.
questions.misconception: Changing mass number in beta-minus decay.

explanation.body: An alpha decay moves two squares left and two down, removing two protons and two neutrons. A beta-minus decay moves one square right and one down, changing a neutron into a proton. Working backwards from Y by two beta-minus steps leads to P, so two successive beta-minus decays take P to Y.

A radioactive source is placed close to the detector and the reading is 532 counts per minute. What will be the reading after two half-lives of the source?
questions.stemText: A detector of ionising radiation gives a background count rate of 24 per minute. A radioactive source is placed close to the detector and the reading is 532 counts per minute. What will be the reading after two half-lives of the source? A 127 B 133 C 151 D 157

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Subtract the background before applying two half-lives and restore it to obtain the detector reading.
questions.misconception: Applying radioactive decay to the background count.

explanation.body: Subtract the background first to get the source count rate of $532-24=508$ counts per minute. After two half-lives, the source count rate is $508/4=127$ counts per minute. Adding back the background gives $127+24=151$ counts per minute.

perOption.A: Reports the decayed source count without restoring the background.
perOption.B: Quarters the entire initial detector reading, including the background.
perOption.C: Correct. It includes the source count after decay and the background.
perOption.D: Quarters the total initial reading and then adds the background again.

questions.stemText: The deviation of $\alpha$-particles by thin metal foils through angles that range from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$. Which of the following could explain this observation? A scattering from bound electrons in the foil B reflection from the foil surface C diffraction from the crystal lattice in the foil D scattering from small and heavy positively charged regions in the foil

questions.difficultyReason: A direct recall of the conclusion of the Rutherford scattering experiment.

explanation.body: The $\alpha$-particles are deflected by the nuclei of the metal atoms in the foil. These nuclei are small, heavy and positively charged, so a few $\alpha$-particles are deflected through large angles, up to $180^\circ$.

perOption.C: The de Broglie wavelength of the $\alpha$-particles is far too small for lattice diffraction to give large-angle deviation.

The half-life of $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ is 5600 years. From a 5.0 g sample of living wood, it was found that the $^{14}\mathrm{C}$ content causes a radioactive count rate of 100 counts per minute. What is the age of a 10 g sample of ancient wood, given that the ancient wood causes a count rate of 50 counts per minute? A 1400 years B 5600 years C 11200 years D 22400 years

explanation.body:
If a 10 g sample of ancient wood gives 50 counts per minute, a 5 g sample of it would give 25 counts per minute.

So for the same mass, the ancient wood's count rate is $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of the living wood's (100 counts per minute). Two half-lives have passed, so the age is $2 \times 5600 = 11200$ years.

perOption.A: Divides the half-life by 4 instead of counting half-lives.
perOption.B: Compares 50 with 100 directly without correcting for the different masses, giving one half-life.

questions.stemText:
When $\alpha$-particles are directed at gold leaf:
1. almost all $\alpha$-particles pass through without deflection
2. a few $\alpha$-particles are deviated through large angles.

What are the reasons for these effects?

| | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|
| A | most $\alpha$-particles have enough energy to pass right through the gold leaf | gold is very dense, so a few low energy $\alpha$-particles bounce back from the gold surface |
| B | most $\alpha$-particles miss all gold atoms | a few $\alpha$-particles bounce off gold atoms |
| C | the gold nucleus is very small so most $\alpha$-particles miss all nuclei | occasionally the path of an $\alpha$-particle is close to a nucleus |
| D | the positive charge in an atom is not concentrated enough to deflect an $\alpha$-particle | occasionally an $\alpha$-particle experiences many small deflections in the same direction |

stemImage.alt: Question 29: When -particles are directed at gold leaf: 1. almost all -particles pass through without deflection 2. a few -particles are deviated through large angles. Wh

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Standard interpretation of Rutherford scattering.
questions.misconception: Thinking alpha particles miss whole atoms or bounce off a surface

explanation.body:
As the nucleus is very small compared with the atom, there is a lot of empty space, so most alpha particles pass straight through.

When an $\alpha$-particle comes very close to a gold nucleus, it experiences a large repulsive force and so can be deviated through a large angle.

perOption.A: Large deflections are caused by electrostatic repulsion from the nucleus, not by particles bouncing off a dense surface.
perOption.B: Alpha particles pass through whole atoms (mostly empty space); they miss nuclei, not atoms, and are repelled rather than bouncing off atoms.
perOption.C: Correct. The tiny nucleus is rarely approached closely, but a close approach gives a large Coulomb repulsion.
perOption.D: Large-angle scattering shows the positive charge is concentrated; it is a single close encounter, not many small deflections.

questions.stemText:
The nuclide $^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U}$ emits an $\alpha$-particle. The resulting nuclide decays by emitting a $\beta$-particle to form a new nuclide.

What are the neutron number and the proton number of the new nuclide?

| | neutron number | proton number |
|---|---|---|
| A | 234 | 91 |
| B | 234 | 90 |
| C | 143 | 91 |
| D | 143 | 90 |

stemImage.alt: Question 30: The nuclide 238 92U emits an -particle. The resulting nuclide decays by emitting a β-particle to form a new nuclide. What are the neutron number and the proton

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Simple bookkeeping of nucleon and proton numbers through two decays.
questions.misconception: Confusing neutron number with nucleon number

explanation.body:
An alpha decay changes the nucleon number by $-4$ and the proton number by $-2$; a beta decay leaves the nucleon number unchanged and adds $+1$ to the proton number.

Hence the new nuclide has nucleon number 234 and proton number $92 - 2 + 1 = 91$.

Its neutron number is therefore $234 - 91 = 143$.

perOption.A: Gives the nucleon number (234) instead of the neutron number.
perOption.B: Gives the nucleon number as the neutron number and ignores the $+1$ in proton number from beta decay.
perOption.C: Correct. Nucleon number 234, proton number 91, so neutron number 143.
perOption.D: Correct neutron number but forgets that beta decay raises the proton number by 1.

Initially, a sample of antimony-124 contains no tin-124.

For this sample, after what period of time will the ratio $\frac{\text{number of tin-124 nuclei}}{\text{number of antimony-124 nuclei}}$ equals 10?

A between 120 days and 180 days
B 180 days
C between 180 days and 240 days
D 240 days

questions.difficultyReason: The daughter-to-parent ratio must be converted to a surviving fraction before using the decay law.
questions.misconception: Confusing the daughter-to-parent ratio with the initial-to-remaining ratio.

explanation.body: There are ten tin nuclei for every remaining antimony nucleus, so the surviving fraction is $N/N_0=1/11$. Using $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln 2/60$ per day gives $\ln(1/11)=-(\ln 2/60)t$. Thus $t=208$ days, between 180 and 240 days.

perOption.B: Stops at three half-lives, when the ratio is 7.
perOption.C: Correct. The ratio reaches 10 after about 208 days.
perOption.D: Waits four half-lives, by which point the ratio is 15.

questions.misconception: Counting free neutrons as bound nucleons.

explanation.body: The energy released equals the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactants. Free neutrons contribute zero binding energy, so $195=143X+90X-235\times7.6$, with energies in MeV. Solving gives $X=8.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
